content.title: About
content.content: The multiple meat sandwich with cheese is a classic sub served at restaurant (1860). It layers ham, salami, roast beef and melted cheese between a soft roll that is lightly toasted to a golden crust.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Multi‑meat sandwiches have been a staple of American diners since the early 20th century.
Combining different meats gives a more complex flavor profile than a single‑meat sandwich.
Cheese is usually chosen for good meltability, such as cheddar or mozzarella, to coat the meat evenly.
The roll is typically made from yeasted dough with a touch of sugar and butter, resulting in a soft, aromatic bun.
At restaurant (1860) the sandwich is served with fries or a fresh side salad.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Meat and cheese provide complete protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Iron source
items.content: Red meat like roast beef supplies iron, important for oxygen transport in the blood.

items.title: Calcium from cheese
items.content: Cheese adds calcium, supporting bone and dental health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Meat is rich in B12, B6 and niacin, which aid nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: Energy dense
items.content: The blend of protein and fat provides lasting satiety and a quick energy boost.

items.title: High saturated fat
items.content: Large amounts of meat and cheese can raise saturated fat intake, which may affect heart health.

items.title: Sodium
items.content: Processed meats and cheese are often salty, a concern for people with hypertension.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Cheese may trigger allergic reactions in individuals with lactose intolerance or milk protein allergy.

items.title: Caloric load
items.content: The sandwich is calorie‑dense; portion control is advisable for weight management.

items.title: Meat quality
items.content: Choose high‑quality, minimally processed meats without excessive preservatives or nitrites.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy the sandwich hot, right after it’s assembled, so the cheese stays melted. It can be cut in half and eaten by hand or with a fork and knife. Common accompaniments are fries, pickles, or a fresh side salad.

content.title: Storage
content.content: If not eaten immediately, store the sandwich in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours. Reheat in an oven or toaster to restore crustiness and warm the cheese before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Passion fruit nectar is a sweet‑tart beverage made from the pulp and juice of passion fruit, diluted with water and sweetened with sugar. It has a vivid tropical aroma and a bright golden‑orange color.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Passion fruit originates from South America but is now cultivated in tropical regions worldwide.
The juice contains over 30 mg of vitamin C per 100 ml, making it a rich source of antioxidants.
Traditionally, passion fruit nectar has been used in Caribbean cuisine as a refreshing drink and dessert ingredient.
Dietary fiber in the fruit pulp supports digestion and gut health.
The nectar is popular in cocktails, smoothies, and marinades for a fruity twist.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C boosts immunity, aids collagen synthesis, and protects cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Flavonoids and carotenoids help neutralize free radicals, supporting heart and vascular health.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Fiber and enzymes in passion fruit aid regular bowel movements and may relieve constipation.

items.title: Mood‑enhancing
items.content: The fragrant aroma of passion fruit has calming effects and can reduce stress levels.

items.title: Source of potassium
items.content: Potassium helps regulate fluid balance and supports normal heart function.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: The nectar contains added sugar, so people with diabetes or those limiting calories should consume it in moderation.

items.title: Passion fruit allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to fruit components.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: High acidity can irritate the stomach lining in persons with gastritis or ulcers.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Passion fruit nectar can be enjoyed chilled on its own, added to cocktails, smoothies, yogurts, desserts, and sauces. It is also used to drizzle fruit salads or as a marinade for seafood.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the nectar in the refrigerator at 2‑4 °C in a sealed container. Once opened, consume within 5‑7 days. Discard if the taste, smell changes or mold appears.

turkey-and-ham-sandwich-on-wheat-with-ch.title: Turkey and Ham Sandwich on Wheat with Cheese

content.title: About
content.content: The sandwich consists of sliced turkey and ham placed between two pieces of whole‑wheat bread, topped with melted cheese. It provides a convenient source of protein, B‑vitamins, and carbohydrates, making it a quick snack or light meal.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Turkey is one of the leanest meats, low in saturated fat.
Ham is often smoked, giving the sandwich a distinctive aroma.
Whole‑wheat bread retains more fiber and micronutrients than white bread.
Cheese adds calcium and helps with vitamin D absorption.
Sandwiches of this type are commonly served in school cafeterias as a balanced option.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Turkey and ham together provide about 20 g of protein per serving, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Poultry supplies vitamin B6 and niacin, important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Fiber from whole‑wheat bread
items.content: Whole‑wheat bread supplies dietary fiber, promoting digestive health.

items.title: Calcium from cheese
items.content: Cheese contributes calcium needed for strong bones and teeth.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Compared with red meat, turkey contains less saturated fat, which is favorable for cardiovascular health.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Cheese may trigger allergic reactions in individuals with lactose intolerance or milk protein allergy.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Ham often contains added salt, so people monitoring sodium intake should watch portion size.

items.title: Preservatives in ham
items.content: Some hams contain nitrites, which are considered undesirable in excess.

items.title: Risk of foodborne illness
items.content: If left at room temperature for more than 2 hours, bacterial growth may increase.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The sandwich is ready to eat straight from the package. For extra flavor you can add fresh vegetables (tomato, lettuce) or mustard. When stored in the fridge, it should be consumed within 24 hours.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep refrigerated at 1‑4 °C in the original packaging or an airtight container. For longer storage (over 3 days) check for off‑odors or texture changes before consumption.

content.title: About
content.content: Vegetables are edible parts of plants such as roots, leaves, stems, and fruits that are commonly used in stews to add flavor, aroma, and nutritional value. Typical stew vegetables include carrots, onions, celery, potatoes, tomatoes, peppers, and zucchini.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Vegetables form the base of many traditional dishes worldwide, such as French "bouillon" and Italian "minestrone".
Their variety of colors and textures makes them ideal for creating visually appealing stews.
Aromatics like onion and garlic release sulfur compounds that enhance the overall scent of the dish.
Seasonal vegetables often have brighter flavors and higher vitamin content than out‑of‑season imports.

items.title: Rich in vitamins and minerals
items.content: Vegetables provide vitamins A, C, K and minerals such as potassium, magnesium, and folate, supporting immune function and heart health.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion, promotes satiety, and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: Vegetables increase the volume of a stew without adding many calories, which is beneficial for weight management.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Pigments like carotenoids and polyphenols protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports gut health
items.content: Prebiotic fibers in certain vegetables foster the growth of beneficial gut bacteria.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to specific vegetables such as tomatoes or peppers.

items.title: Pesticide residues
items.content: Improperly washed vegetables can retain pesticide residues; thorough rinsing or choosing organic produce is recommended.

items.title: Oxalate overload
items.content: Vegetables high in oxalates, like spinach and beetroot, may contribute to kidney stone formation in susceptible people.

content.title: How to Cook
content.content: Vegetables are usually diced or sliced and sautéed briefly in a little oil until softened, then combined with broth, meat or legumes and simmered over low heat. For deeper flavor add tomato paste, herbs (thyme, rosemary) and spices.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store fresh vegetables in the refrigerator’s crisper drawer in perforated bags. Root vegetables (carrots, potatoes) keep best in a cool, dark place. Cooked vegetable mixtures should be kept in an airtight container for 3‑4 days.
